title: Calling a messy integral zero without integrating
problem: An AI tutor evaluated \(\int_{-2}^{2} x^3 \cos(x^2)\, dx\) without ever finding an antiderivative. Tap a slip if you spot one, or call it clean.
steps: Let \(f(x) = x^3 \cos(x^2)\), which is continuous everywhere on \([-2, 2]\).
So \(f\) is an odd function integrated over the symmetric interval \([-2, 2]\).
Splitting at \(0\), the integral over \([-2, 0]\) is the exact negative of the integral over \([0, 2]\).
Therefore \(\int_{-2}^{2} x^3 \cos(x^2)\, dx = 0\), with no antiderivative needed.

meta.topic: Odd symmetry on a symmetric definite integral
meta.blurb: It never integrated a single term and just wrote down \(0\) — clever shortcut or total bluff?

explanation: Skipping the antiderivative sounds lazy, except \(x^3\) is odd and \(\cos(x^2)\) is even, so their product is strictly odd and cancels out over \([-2, 2]\).
